title: Celsus mixes sect with sect
source_text: Εἶτ᾿ οἶμαι φύρων αἱρέσεις αἱρέσεσι καὶ μὴ ἐπισημειούμενος ὅτι τάδε μὲν ἄλλης αἱρέσεώς ἐστι τάδε δὲ ἄλλης, τὰ πρὸς Μαρκίωνα ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν ἀπορούμενα προφέρει, τάχα καὶ τούτων παρακούσας ἀπό τινων εὐτελῶς καὶ ἰδιωτικῶς [ἐγκαλεῖ τῶν] ἐγκαλούντων λόγῳ. οὐ μὴν πάνυ συνετῶς. ἐκτιθέμενος οὖν τὰ κατὰ Μαρκίωνος λεγόμενα καὶ μὴ ἐπισημειωσάμενος ὅτι πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγει φησί· τί δὲ λάθρα πέμπει καὶ διαφθείρει τὰ τούτου δημιουργήματα; τί δὲ εἰσβιάζεται κρύφα καὶ παραπείθει καὶ πλανᾷ; τί δὲ τοὺς ὑπὸ τούτου κατεγνωσμένους ἢ κατηραμένους, ὥς φατε, ψυχαγωγεῖ καὶ δίκην ἀνδραποδιστοῦ τινος ὑπεξάγει; τί δὲ ἀποδιδράσκειν ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου διδάσκει; τί δὲ φεύγειν τὸν πατέρα; τί δ᾿ αὐτὸς εἰσποιεῖται, μὴ συγχωροῦντος τοῦ πατρός; τί δ᾿ ἐπαγγέλλεται τῶν ἀλλοτρίων εἶναι πατήρ; καὶ ἐπιφέρει γε αὐτοῖς οἱονεὶ θαυμαστικῶς τό· σεμνός γε ὁ θεὸς τῶν παρ᾿ ἄλλῳ καταδίκων ἁμαρτωλῶν καὶ ἀκλήρων καὶ, ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι, σκυβάλων ἐπιθυμῶν εἶναι πατὴρ, καὶ ὅν γε ἐξέπεμψεν, αὐτοῦ ὑπεξάγοντα, τοῦτον ἁλόντα ἐκδικῆσαι μὴ δυνάμενος. ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις ὡσπερεὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς τοὺς ὁμολογοῦντας οὐκ ἀλλοτρίου τινὸς εἶναι καὶ ξένου θεοῦ τόνδε τὸν κόσμον, τοιαῦτά φησιν· εἰ δὲ (αὐτοῦ) ταῦτ᾿ ἔστιν ἔργα, πῶς μὲν κακὰ ὁ θεὸς ἐποίει; πῶς δὲ πείθειν καὶ νουθετεῖν ἀδυνατεῖ; πῶς δ᾿ ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἀχαρίστοις καὶ πονηροῖς γενομένοις μεταμέλει καὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τέχνην μέμφεται καὶ μισεῖ καὶ ἀπειλεῖ καὶ φθείρει τὰ ἴδια ἔκγονα; ἢ ποῖ ποτε ὑπεξάγει τοῦ κόσμου τοῦδε ὃν ἐποίησεν αὐτός; δοκεῖ δή μοι καὶ ἐν τούτοις μὴ σαφηνίζων, τίνα ἐστὶ τὰ κακὰ, καίτοι γε καὶ ἐν Ἕλλησι πολλῶν αἱρέσεων γενομένων περὶ ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν, συναρπάζων ὡς ἀκόλουθον ἡμῖν, τοῖς φάσκουσιν ἔργα τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ εἶναι καὶ τόνδε τὸν κόσμον, τὸ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς κακῶν εἶναι ποιητὴν τὸν θεόν. ἐχέτω μὲν οὖν ὅπως ποτὲ ἔχει τὰ περὶ τῶν κακῶν, πότερον ὁ θεὸς αὐτὰ πεποίηκεν ἢ μὴ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ παρακολουθήσεως γεγένηται τῆς πρὸς τὰ προηγούμενα· θαυμάζω δὲ εἰ μὴ ὅπερ ἡμῖν, τοῖς φάσκουσιν ἔργα εἶναι τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ καὶ τόνδε τὸν κόσμον, οἴεται ἀκολουθεῖν περὶ τοῦ τὸν θεὸν τὰ κακὰ πεποιηκέναι, ἀκολουθεῖ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ οἷς λέγει καὶ αὐτός. εἴποι γὰρ ἄν τις πρὸς τὸν Κέλσον· εἰ αὐτοῦ ταῦτ᾿ ἔστιν ἔργα, πῶς μὲν κακὰ ὁ θεὸς ἐποίει; πῶς δὲ πείθειν καὶ νουθετεῖν ἀδυνατεῖ; κακία δὲ ἡ μεγίστη ἐν λόγοις ἐστὶν, ὅτε ἐγκαλεῖ τις τοῖς ἑτεροδόξοις περί τινων δογμάτων ὡς οὐχ ὑγιῶν, πολλῷ πρότερον αὐτὸς ἔχων τὰ ἐγκλήματα ἐν τοῖς ἰδίοις δόγμασιν.
pass_a_gloss: Then, I think, mixing (φύρω) sects (αἱρέσεις) with sects and not noting (ἐπισημειόομαι) that these are of one sect and those of another, he brings forward (προφέρω) the difficulties raised (ἀπορέω) by us against Marcion, perhaps having misheard (παρακούω) these too from some who cheaply (εὐτελῶς) and amateurishly (ἰδιωτικῶς) charge (ἐγκαλέω) the teaching (λόγῳ); not, however, very intelligently (συνετῶς). Setting out then the things said against Marcion and not noting that he speaks against him, he says: ‘Why does he send secretly (λάθρα) and destroy (διαφθείρω) the creations (δημιουργήματα) of this one? Why does he force his way in (εἰσβιάζομαι) covertly (κρύφα) and persuade aside (παραπείθω) and lead astray (πλανάω)? Why does he lure (ψυχαγωγέω) those condemned (καταγινώσκω) or cursed (καταράομαι) by this one, as you say, and like a kidnapper (ἀνδραποδιστής) steal them away (ὑπεξάγω)? Why does he teach to run away (ἀποδιδράσκω) from the lord/master (κύριος)? Why to flee the father? Why does he himself adopt (εἰσποιέομαι) them, the father not consenting (συγχωρέω)? Why does he profess (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to be father of those belonging to another (ἀλλότριοι)?’ And he adds to them as in wonder (θαυμαστικῶς): ‘August (σεμνός) indeed the god, desiring to be father of sinners condemned (κατάδικοι) by another, and of the disinherited (ἄκληροι) and, as they themselves say, of refuse (σκύβαλα); and the one whom he sent out, stealing away from him, this one when caught (ἁλίσκομαι) unable to avenge (ἐκδικέω).’ Next after these, as if to us who confess that this world is not of some foreign (ἀλλότριος) and strange (ξένος) god, he says such things: ‘But if these are his works (ἔργα), how did God make evils (κακά)? How is he unable (ἀδυνατέω) to persuade (πείθω) and admonish (νουθετέω)? How does he repent (μεταμέλει) over them become ungrateful (ἀχάριστοι) and wicked (πονηροί), and blame (μέμφομαι) his own craft (τέχνη), and hate, and threaten, and destroy (φθείρω) his own offspring (ἔκγονα)? Or where (ποῖ) does he lead them away out of this world which he himself made?’ It seems to me that in these too, not making clear (σαφηνίζω) what the evils are, although among Greeks too many schools (αἱρέσεις) have arisen about goods and evils, he snatches (συναρπάζω) as a consequence (ἀκόλουθον) for us, who say this world too is works of the God over all, that on our account God is maker (ποιητής) of evils. Let the matter of evils be however it is, whether God has made them or not, but they have come about by consequence (παρακολούθησις) upon the principal things (τὰ προηγούμενα); but I wonder if what he thinks follows for us, who say this world too is works of the God over all, concerning God’s having made evils, does not follow as far as concerns what he himself also says. For one might say to Celsus: ‘If these are his works, how did God make evils? How is he unable to persuade and admonish?’ And the greatest vice (κακία) in arguments is when someone charges those of other opinion (ἑτερόδοξοι) concerning some doctrines (δόγματα) as not sound (ὑγιής), himself much sooner having the charges (ἐγκλήματα) in his own doctrines.
pass_b_english: Then, I think, mixing up sects with sects and not noting that these views belong to one sect and those to another, he brings forward the difficulties we raise against Marcion. Perhaps he misheard these too from some who attack that teaching cheaply and like amateurs, and not very intelligently at that. So, setting out what is said against Marcion, and without noting that he is speaking against him, he says: “Why does he send in secret and destroy the works this one has made? Why does he force his way in covertly, and entice, and lead astray? Why does he beguile those whom this one has condemned or cursed, as you say, and spirit them away like some kidnapper? Why does he teach them to run away from the Master? Why to flee the Father? Why does he adopt them himself, without the Father’s consent? Why does he profess to be the father of those who belong to another?”

And he adds to these words, as if in astonishment: “A fine God indeed, who longs to be father of sinners condemned by another, of the disinherited, and, as they themselves say, of refuse; and who could not avenge the one he sent to steal them away from the other, when that one was caught!”

Next after these, as if speaking to us who confess that this world does not belong to some foreign and strange god, he says something like this: “But if these are his works, how did God make evils? How is he unable to persuade and admonish? How does he repent over them when they have become ungrateful and wicked, and find fault with his own craftsmanship, and hate, and threaten, and destroy his own offspring (Genesis 6:6–7)? Or where does he lead them away to, out of this world which he himself made?”

It seems to me that here too he does not make clear what evils are, although among the Greeks too there have been many schools of thought about goods and evils. Instead he jumps to the conclusion that, on our teaching, God is the maker of evils, as though this followed for us, who say that this world too is the work of the God over all. Let the question of evils stand however it stands, whether God made them, or whether instead they came about as a by-product of what he primarily made. But I should be surprised if what he thinks follows for us, who say that this world too is the work of the God over all, namely that God has made evils, does not follow for him as well, judging by what he himself says. For one might say to Celsus: “If these are his works, how did God make evils? How is he unable to persuade and admonish?” And the worst fault in argument is to accuse people of other opinions of holding certain doctrines that are unsound, when one’s own doctrines are open to those very charges, and far more so.

choices.choice: ‘The difficulties we raise against Marcion’: ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν = by us, the Church. The edition brackets [ἐγκαλεῖ τῶν] before ἐγκαλούντων; translated without it. οὐ μὴν πάνυ συνετῶς may qualify either Celsus’s mishearing or the amateur critics; rendered so as to attach to the critics, the nearer construction. In Celsus’s questions ‘this one’ (τούτου) and ‘the Master’ (τοῦ κυρίου, in a runaway-slave image with ἀποδιδράσκειν) and ‘the Father’ are the Creator, and ‘he’ is Marcion’s higher god who sends his Son; capitalised because Origen holds that the Creator is God the Father, and ‘A fine God’ (ironic σεμνός) is capitalised because it means the Father of Christ in Marcion’s scheme. ‘The father of those who belong to another’: lowercase, a general claim to fatherhood. ‘Refuse’ (σκύβαλα): possibly an echo of Christian self-description (compare 1 Corinthians 4:13 or Philippians 3:8), not cited inline because the reference is uncertain. ‘The one he sent… when that one was caught’: αὐτοῦ (‘from him’) refers to the Creator, and ἁλόντα points to the arrest and death of Christ. (αὐτοῦ) in Celsus’s next question is an editorial supplement. The repenting and destroying God alludes to the Flood story, Genesis 6:6–7 (the LXX there reads ἐνεθυμήθη, ‘took to heart’, not ‘repented’); cited inline as a clear allusion in Celsus’s words. ‘By-product of what was primarily made’ for ἐκ παρακολουθήσεως… πρὸς τὰ προηγούμενα (Stoic terminology for side-effects of a primary intention).
title ‘Celsus Confuses Marcion with the Church’ → ‘Celsus Mixes Sect with Sect’ (Origen’s own charge, φύρων αἱρέσεις αἱρέσεσι)
‘seduce’ → ‘entice’ (παραπείθει); ‘lure away … steal them away’ → ‘beguile … spirit them away like some kidnapper’ (ψυχαγωγεῖ, ὑπεξάγει, τινος kept)
‘run away from the Lord’ → ‘run away from the Master’: ἀποδιδράσκειν ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου is Celsus’s runaway-slave image; capital M because it means the Creator
‘hastily seizes on it as a consequence for us … that’ → ‘jumps to the conclusion that … as though this followed for us’ (συναρπάζων ὡς ἀκόλουθον; stiff Greek order fixed)
‘whether God made them or not but they came about’ → ‘whether God made them, or whether instead they came about’
‘the same charges, and far sooner’ → ‘those very charges, and far more so’ (πολλῷ πρότερον)
